entities.name: Chamber of Peers
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Chamber of Peers (Chambre des Pairs), France's upper legislative chamber operating during the Restoration (1814-1830) and July Monarchy (1830-1848) periods, was the French equivalent of the British House of Lords — a hereditary and appointed upper house comprising the traditional aristocracy, Napoleonic nobility, and royal appointees — serving as the institutional embodiment of the Orleanist constitutional monarchy's attempt to balance royal prerogative with representative government in post-Napoleonic France.

The Chamber of Peers was established by the Constitutional Charter of 1814, which Louis XVIII granted upon his restoration after Napoleon's defeat. It was modeled on the British House of Lords, serving alongside the elected Chamber of Deputies as France's bicameral legislature. Peers (pairs de France) held their positions hereditarily or by royal appointment for life; the chamber included both 'old nobility' of pre-Revolutionary France and 'new men' ennobled by Napoleon. This mixture reflected the Restoration's attempt to reconcile the Old Regime with the Napoleonic legacy.

The Chamber of Peers' most dramatic moments came as a court: it tried the marshals of Napoleon condemned by the Restoration (Michel Ney was condemned to death, 1815), tried the Ultraroyalist ministers of Charles X after the 1830 July Revolution, and served as an arena for France's political class to negotiate the balance between royalist and constitutional principles. The Second Republic (1848) abolished the Chamber of Peers, replacing it with a unicameral National Assembly, ending the 34-year experiment in French upper chamber conservatism.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: France's Chamber of Peers — the Restoration-era upper house that tried Napoleon's marshals, balanced old and new nobility, and embodied the constitutional monarchy experiment between Napoleonic empire and Republican revolution — is a significant institution in France's complex 19th-century political history.
